Spatial sampling with SamplingStrata

Marco Ballin, Giulio Barcaroli

2026-11-20

Source: vignettes/spatial.Rmd
spatial.Rmd

Optimization with the spatial method

Let us suppose we want to design a sample survey with kkZZ target variables, each one of them correlated to one or more of the available YY frame variables.

When frame units are georeferenced or geocoded, the presence of spatial auto-correlation can be investigated. This can be done by executing for instance the Moran test on the target variables: if the null hypothesis is rejected (i.e. the hypothesis of the presence of spatial auto-correlation is accepted) then we should take into account also this variance component.

As indicated by de Gruijter et al. (2016) and de Gruijter et al. (2019), in case ZZ is the target variable, omitting as negligible the fpc factor, the sampling variance of its estimated mean is:

V(Z‾̂)=∑h=1H(Nh/N)2Sh2/nh(1) V(\hat{\bar{Z}}) = \sum_{h=1}^{H}(N_{h}/N)^{2} S_{h}^{2}/n_{h} \qquad (1)

We can write the variance in each stratum hh as:

Sh2=1Nh2∑i=1Nh−1∑j=i+1Nh(zi−zj)2(2) S_{h}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{N_{h}^{2}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{h-1}}\sum_{j=i+1}^{N_{h}}(z_{i}-z_{j})^{2} \qquad (2)

The optimal determination of strata is obtained by minimizing the quantity OO:

O=∑h=1H1Nh2{∑i=1Nh−1∑j=i+1Nh(zi−zj)2}1/2(3) O = \sum_{h=1}^{H} \dfrac{1}{N_{h}^{2}} \{ \sum_{i=1}^{N_{h-1}} \sum_{j=i+1}^{N_{h}} (z_{i}-z_{j})^{2}\}^{1/2} \qquad (3)

Obviously, values zz are not known, but only their predictions z̃\tilde{z}, obtained by means of a model (for instance a regression or a kriging model), together with the variances of their prediction errors eie_{i}. Assuming that the predictions are unbiased and that the errors are uncorrelated with the predictions (as for a well-calibrated model), de Gruijter et al. (2015, Eq. 10) and de Gruijter et al. (2016, Eq. 15) show that the model expectation of (zi−zj)2(z_{i}-z_{j})^{2}, conditional on the predictions, is

Dij2=(z̃i−z̃j)2+V(ei)+V(ej)−2Cov(ei,ej)(4) D_{ij}^{2} = (\tilde{z}_{i}-\tilde{z}_{j})^{2} + V(e_{i}) + V(e_{j}) - 2Cov(e_{i},e_{j}) \qquad (4)

that can be substituted to (zi−zj)2(z_{i}-z_{j})^{2} in Equations (2) and (3). The term V(ei)+V(ej)V(e_{i}) + V(e_{j}) compensates for the levelling (smoothing) effect of the predictions, whose variance is smaller than that of the true values. The spatial auto-correlation component is contained in the term Cov(ei,ej)Cov(e_{i},e_{j}).

Note. de Gruijter et al. (2015, Eq. 11) and de Gruijter et al. (2019, Eq. 2) also divide the first term by the coefficient of determination R2R^{2} of the prediction model, in order to correct for the levelling effect. Under the assumptions above this correction is already made by the error variances, so that applying both counts the error variance twice: averaging over the pairs of units, Var(z̃)/R2+V‾(e)=Var(z)+(1−R2)Var(z)Var(\tilde{z})/R^{2} + \bar{V}(e) = Var(z) + (1-R^{2})Var(z). From this version on, SamplingStrata uses Equation (4) by default (parameter fitting = 1). The two corrections are alternatives:

  • additive correction (default): prediction-error variances in the frame and fitting = 1;
  • rescaling correction: fitting equal to the R2R^{2} of the prediction model (computed as 1−SSE/SST1 - SSE/SST, preferably on validation data) and prediction-error variances set to zero in the frame.

Using fitting < 1 together with positive prediction-error variances is rejected: the functions stop with an error. If only the R2R^{2} of the prediction model is known, the additive correction can still be used, with fitting = 1 and a constant prediction-error variance s2=Var(z̃)(1−R2)/R2s^{2} = Var(\tilde{z})(1-R^{2})/R^{2} in the frame. On average over the population this gives the same total variance as the rescaling correction, but within the strata it does not assume that the stratification can remove the error variance, as the rescaling Sh2(z̃)/R2S^{2}_{h}(\tilde{z})/R^{2} does (when the predictions in a stratum are almost constant, the rescaled variance goes to zero, while the error variance remains).

The covariance between the prediction errors of two distinct units is modelled as

Cov(ei,ej)=(1−ν)sisjρ(dij)(5) Cov(e_{i},e_{j}) = (1-\nu) \, s_{i} \, s_{j} \, \rho(d_{ij}) \qquad (5)

so that

Dij2=(z̃i−z̃j)2+(si2+sj2)−2(1−ν)sisjρ(dij)(6) D_{ij}^{2} = (\tilde{z}_{i}-\tilde{z}_{j})^{2} + (s_{i}^{2} + s_{j}^{2}) - 2 (1-\nu) \, s_{i} \, s_{j} \, \rho(d_{ij}) \qquad (6)

where:

  • dijd_{ij} is the Euclidean distance between units ii and jj (calculated using their geographical coordinates, that must be expressed in meters);
  • si2s_{i}^{2} and sj2s_{j}^{2} are the variances of the prediction errors in the single points;
  • ρ(d)\rho(d) is the correlation function of the variogram model fitted on the prediction errors (parameter vgm_model: exponential, spherical or gaussian), as explained in Section Variogram models;
  • rr (parameter range) and ν\nu (parameter nugget) describe the spatial correlation of the prediction errors, and are obtained from their variogram;
  • κ\kappa (parameter kappa, used by the exponential and gaussian models) depends on how the range rr is defined, as explained in Section Choice of the parameter kappa;
  • ν=c0/(c0+c1)\nu = c_{0}/(c_{0}+c_{1}) is the relative nugget: the share of the error variance (micro-scale variability and measurement error) that is not spatially correlated, even between units at very short distance. With ν=0\nu = 0 (default) two very close units have almost perfectly correlated errors; with a large nugget the reduction of variance due to the spatial correlation is correspondingly smaller. The nugget is given in relative terms because the scale of the error variance is already given, unit by unit, by si2s_{i}^{2}.

With range = 0, or nugget = 1, there is no spatial correlation, and Equation (6) reduces to the non-spatial case. Since the correlation is non-negative, with fitting = 1 the spatial component can only reduce the variance in the strata.

Variogram models

The correlation function ρ(d)\rho(d) in Equation (5) must be coherent with the model of the variogram fitted on the prediction errors. The parameter vgm_model of optimStrata (and of optimizeStrataSpatial, KmeansSolutionSpatial, buildStrataDFSpatial and aggrStrataSpatial) selects one of the most commonly used models:

vgm_model ρ(d)\rho(d) Notes
"exponential" (default), or "Exp" e−κd/re^{-\kappa\, d/r} Never exactly 0; with κ=3\kappa = 3, ρ(r)≈0.05\rho(r) \approx 0.05 (practical range)
"spherical", or "Sph" 1−1.5dr+0.5(dr)31 - 1.5\,\frac{d}{r} + 0.5\left(\frac{d}{r}\right)^{3} for d<rd < r, and 0 for d≥rd \geq r Exactly 0 at and beyond the range; κ\kappa is not used
"gaussian", or "Gau" e−κ(d/r)2e^{-\kappa\,(d/r)^{2}} Very smooth near the origin; with κ=3\kappa = 3, ρ(r)≈0.05\rho(r) \approx 0.05 (practical range)

The abbreviations are the names of the models in gstat and automap, so that the model of a fitted variogram can be passed directly (for instance as.character(kriging_lead$var_model$model[2])). One model can be given for all the target variables, or one for each of them (as for range and nugget); with optimStrata and optimizeStrataSpatial a dataframe with one row per domain can also be given.

For the spherical model, rr is the distance at which the variogram reaches the sill, i.e. the column range of the Sph row of a model fitted with gstat or automap. Other models (for instance the Matern model, of which the exponential and the gaussian are particular cases) are not available.

Choice of the parameter kappa

The exponential variogram of the prediction errors is

γ(d)=c0+c1(1−e−d/a)\gamma(d) = c_{0} + c_{1}\left(1 - e^{-d/a}\right)

and the corresponding correlation between two units at distance dd is (1−ν)e−d/a(1-\nu)\,e^{-d/a}. Unlike the spherical model, the exponential model never reaches its sill: the parameter aa is a scale parameter, not a distance beyond which the correlation is zero. At distance aa the correlation is still e−1≈0.37e^{-1} \approx 0.37; it falls to 5% at d=aln⁡20≈3ad = a \ln 20 \approx 3a, the distance conventionally called practical (or effective) range.

Software and papers report either of the two quantities as “range”. The parameter kappa makes the formula independent of the convention: the correlation is computed as e−κd/re^{-\kappa\, d/r}, so that

The value given as range is Typical source kappa
the parameter aa of the exponential model gstat::fit.variogram, automap::autofitVariogram / autoKrige (column range of the Exp row of the fitted model) 1
the practical range (≈3a\approx 3a), i.e. the distance at which the variogram reaches about 95% of the sill software or papers that report the practical range, a range read on a variogram plot as the distance at which it levels off, Ospats and de Gruijter et al. (2019) (who use e−3d/rangee^{-3d/\mathrm{range}}) 3

With kappa = 1 and r=ar = a, or with kappa = 3 and r=3ar = 3a, the correlation is the same. Using the wrong value changes the distance of correlation by a factor of 3: kappa = 1 with the practical range makes the errors correlated over a distance three times too long, and therefore overstates the reduction of the variance due to the spatial component; kappa = 3 with the parameter aa understates it.

Other values are admissible: in general, if range is the distance at which the correlation falls to pp, then κ=−ln⁡p\kappa = -\ln p (for instance ln⁡10≈2.3\ln 10 \approx 2.3 for 10%). Since 1 and 3 are the usual conventions, a value of kappa other than 1 and 3 gives a warning; a value equal to or lower than 0 gives an error, because with κ=0\kappa = 0 the errors would be perfectly correlated at any distance, and with κ<0\kappa < 0 the correlation would increase with the distance.

The default value of kappa is 3, for compatibility with the previous versions of the package. When the range is taken from gstat or automap, as in the example below, kappa = 1 must be set explicitly.

The same convention holds for the gaussian model, whose variogram in gstat is γ(d)=c0+c1(1−e−(d/a)2)\gamma(d) = c_{0} + c_{1}\left(1 - e^{-(d/a)^{2}}\right): kappa = 1 with r=ar = a, kappa = 3 with the practical range r=3ar = \sqrt{3}\,a. The spherical model has no such ambiguity, and kappa is ignored.

Estimation of range and nugget

The range and the nugget should be estimated on the variogram of the prediction errors, i.e. of the out-of-sample residuals (observed minus predicted values, from cross-validation or independent validation data): at the calibration points the residuals of a kriging model are close to zero and not informative about the prediction error. When the variances si2s_{i}^{2} vary much across the units, the variogram should be computed on the standardised residuals (zi−z̃i)/si(z_{i}-\tilde{z}_{i})/s_{i}, whose structure is the one assumed in Equation (5).

To summarize, when frame units can be geo-referenced, the proposed procedure is the following:

  • acquire coordinates of the geographic location of the units in the population of interest;
  • fit a kriging model (or any other spatial model) on data for each ZZ;
  • obtain predicted values together with prediction-error variances for each ZZ and associate them to each unit in the frame;
  • fit a variogram model (exponential, spherical or gaussian) to the prediction errors, estimate its range and relative nugget, and set vgm_model accordingly; with the exponential and gaussian models, set kappa according to the definition of the range (1 for the range parameter, 3 for the practical range);
  • perform the optimization step with fitting = 1.

Example

In order to illustrate the “spatial” method, we make use of a dataset generally employed as an example of spatially correlated phenomena (in this case, the concentration of four heavy metals in a portion of the river Meuse). This dataset comes with the library “sp”:

library(sp)
# locations (155 observed points)
data("meuse")
# grid of points (3103)
data("meuse.grid")
meuse.grid$id <- c(1:nrow(meuse.grid))
coordinates(meuse)<-c("x","y")
coordinates(meuse.grid)<-c("x","y")

We analyse the territorial distribution of the lead and zinc concentration, and model (by using the universal kriging) their relations with distance from the river, using the subset of 155 points on which these values have been jointly observed. We first fit an exponential variogram (vgm_model = "exponential"); a spherical variogram is considered later, for comparison:

library(automap)
kriging_lead = autoKrige(log(lead) ~ dist, meuse, meuse.grid, model = "Exp")
## [using universal kriging]
plot(kriging_lead,sp.layout = NULL, justPosition = TRUE)

kriging_zinc = autoKrige(log(zinc) ~ dist, meuse, meuse.grid, model = "Exp")
## [using universal kriging]
plot(kriging_zinc, sp.layout = list(pts = list("sp.points", meuse)))

From the fitted variograms we take the range parameter aa of the exponential model (to be used with kappa = 1) and the relative nugget c0/(c0+c1)c_{0}/(c_{0}+c_{1}):

kriging_lead$var_model
##   model      psill    range
## 1   Nug 0.05972538   0.0000
## 2   Exp 0.24751270 392.6089
range_lead  <- kriging_lead$var_model$range[2]
nugget_lead <- kriging_lead$var_model$psill[1] / sum(kriging_lead$var_model$psill)
kriging_zinc$var_model
##   model      psill    range
## 1   Nug 0.04525859   0.0000
## 2   Exp 0.24392958 292.6641
range_zinc  <- kriging_zinc$var_model$range[2]
nugget_zinc <- kriging_zinc$var_model$psill[1] / sum(kriging_zinc$var_model$psill)
c(range_lead = range_lead, nugget_lead = nugget_lead)
##  range_lead nugget_lead 
## 392.6088890   0.1943945
c(range_zinc = range_zinc, nugget_zinc = nugget_zinc)
##  range_zinc nugget_zinc 
## 292.6641200   0.1565022

For simplicity, in this example range and nugget are taken from the variograms fitted by the kriging models, i.e. from the residuals of the trend on the distance from the river. In real applications they should be estimated on the variogram of the out-of-sample prediction errors (for instance from the cross-validation residuals given by gstat::krige.cv), as explained above. The fitting parameter is not needed: the prediction-error variances produced by kriging are in the frame, so the additive correction (fitting = 1, the default) applies.

Using these kriging models, we are able to predict the values of lead and zinc concentration on the totality of the 3,103 points in the Meuse territory:

df <- NULL
df$id <- meuse.grid$id
df$lead.pred <- kriging_lead$krige_output@data$var1.pred
df$lead.var <- kriging_lead$krige_output@data$var1.var
df$zinc.pred <- kriging_zinc$krige_output@data$var1.pred
df$zinc.var <- kriging_zinc$krige_output@data$var1.var
df$lon <- meuse.grid$x
df$lat <- meuse.grid$y
df$dom1 <- 1
df <- as.data.frame(df)
head(df)
##   id lead.pred  lead.var zinc.pred  zinc.var    lon    lat dom1
## 1  1  5.517159 0.2083630  6.712998 0.2151660 181180 333740    1
## 2  2  5.550284 0.1791932  6.766572 0.1832443 181140 333700    1
## 3  3  5.494689 0.1884051  6.682140 0.1941760 181180 333700    1
## 4  4  5.396745 0.1974743  6.544145 0.2043451 181220 333700    1
## 5  5  5.592130 0.1436757  6.837125 0.1404987 181100 333660    1
## 6  6  5.531484 0.1555376  6.744487 0.1562711 181140 333660    1

The aim is now to produce the optimal stratification of the 3,103 points under a precision constraint of 1% on the target estimates of the mean lead and zinc concentrations:

library(SamplingStrata)
frame <- buildFrameSpatial(df=df,
                      id="id",
                      X=c("lead.pred","zinc.pred"),
                      Y=c("lead.pred","zinc.pred"),
                      variance=c("lead.var","zinc.var"),
                      lon="lon",
                      lat="lat",
                      domainvalue = "dom1")
cv <- as.data.frame(list(DOM=rep("DOM1",1),
                         CV1=rep(0.01,1),
                         CV2=rep(0.01,1),
                         domainvalue=c(1:1) ))

To this aim, we carry out the optimization step by indicating the method spatial, with the range and the relative nugget of the two variograms (fitting is omitted, i.e. equal to 1):

set.seed(1234)
solution_exp <- optimStrata (
  method = "spatial",
  errors=cv, 
  framesamp=frame,
  iter = 25,
  pops = 10,
  nStrata = 5,
  range = c(range_lead, range_zinc),
  nugget = c(nugget_lead, nugget_zinc),
  kappa = 1,
  vgm_model = "exponential",   # model fitted by autoKrige (default)
  writeFiles = FALSE,
  showPlot = FALSE,
  parallel = FALSE)
## 
## Input data have been checked and are compliant with requirements
## 
##  *** Domain :  1   1
##  Number of strata :  3103
##  *** Sample cost:  68.56499
##  *** Number of strata:  5

## 
##  *** Sample size :  69
##  *** Number of strata :  5
## ---------------------------
n_exp <- sum(solution_exp$aggr_strata$SOLUZ)
n_exp
## [1] 68.56499

Comparison with a spherical variogram

The same steps can be repeated with a spherical variogram. The choice of the model affects both the frame, because the kriging predictions and their error variances depend on the variogram, and the correlation function ρ(d)\rho(d) used in the optimization (Section Variogram models):

kriging_lead_sph = autoKrige(log(lead) ~ dist, meuse, meuse.grid, model = "Sph")
## [using universal kriging]
kriging_zinc_sph = autoKrige(log(zinc) ~ dist, meuse, meuse.grid, model = "Sph")
## [using universal kriging]
kriging_lead_sph$var_model
##   model      psill    range
## 1   Nug 0.07896613   0.0000
## 2   Sph 0.21142964 852.9118
kriging_zinc_sph$var_model
##   model      psill    range
## 1   Nug 0.07473912   0.0000
## 2   Sph 0.20518590 723.9555
range_lead_sph  <- kriging_lead_sph$var_model$range[2]
nugget_lead_sph <- kriging_lead_sph$var_model$psill[1] / sum(kriging_lead_sph$var_model$psill)
range_zinc_sph  <- kriging_zinc_sph$var_model$range[2]
nugget_zinc_sph <- kriging_zinc_sph$var_model$psill[1] / sum(kriging_zinc_sph$var_model$psill)

For the spherical model range is the distance at which the variogram reaches the sill, and kappa is not needed. We build the frame with the predictions and variances of the spherical kriging, and optimize with vgm_model = "spherical", keeping the same seed and the same parameters of the genetic algorithm:

df_sph <- df
df_sph$lead.pred <- kriging_lead_sph$krige_output@data$var1.pred
df_sph$lead.var  <- kriging_lead_sph$krige_output@data$var1.var
df_sph$zinc.pred <- kriging_zinc_sph$krige_output@data$var1.pred
df_sph$zinc.var  <- kriging_zinc_sph$krige_output@data$var1.var
frame_sph <- buildFrameSpatial(df=df_sph,
                      id="id",
                      X=c("lead.pred","zinc.pred"),
                      Y=c("lead.pred","zinc.pred"),
                      variance=c("lead.var","zinc.var"),
                      lon="lon",
                      lat="lat",
                      domainvalue = "dom1")
set.seed(5678)
solution_sph <- optimStrata (
  method = "spatial",
  errors=cv, 
  framesamp=frame_sph,
  iter = 25,
  pops = 10,
  nStrata = 5,
  range = c(range_lead_sph, range_zinc_sph),
  nugget = c(nugget_lead_sph, nugget_zinc_sph),
  vgm_model = "spherical",
  writeFiles = FALSE,
  showPlot = FALSE,
  parallel = FALSE)
## 
## Input data have been checked and are compliant with requirements
## 
##  *** Domain :  1   1
##  Number of strata :  3103
##  *** Sample cost:  68.97252
##  *** Number of strata:  5

## 
##  *** Sample size :  69
##  *** Number of strata :  5
## ---------------------------
n_sph <- sum(solution_sph$aggr_strata$SOLUZ)

The two solutions can be compared in terms of sample size and number of strata. The table also reports the error sum of squares of the fit of the two variograms (sserr, as given by autoKrige):

data.frame(variogram = c("exponential", "spherical"),
           sample_size = round(c(n_exp, n_sph), 1),
           sserr_lead = c(kriging_lead$sserr, kriging_lead_sph$sserr),
           sserr_zinc = c(kriging_zinc$sserr, kriging_zinc_sph$sserr))
##     variogram sample_size   sserr_lead   sserr_zinc
## 1 exponential        68.6 2.393262e-05 6.346710e-06
## 2   spherical        69.0 1.868241e-05 5.907235e-06

In this example the two variogram models lead to practically the same sample size (about 69 units, with 5 strata in both cases): the design is not sensitive to the choice between the exponential and the spherical model. The sample is selected from the solution with the smaller sample size:

best <- if (n_sph < n_exp) "spherical" else "exponential"
best
## [1] "exponential"
solution <- if (best == "spherical") solution_sph else solution_exp
framenew <- solution$framenew
outstrata <- solution$aggr_strata

In general, the sample size is not a criterion for the choice of the variogram model: a model that implies a stronger spatial correlation of the errors gives smaller samples, and if it is not supported by the data the precision constraints may not be met. The model should be chosen on the basis of the fit of the variogram of the prediction errors (for instance sserr, or the cross-validation of the kriging model); the comparison of the sample sizes shows how sensitive the design is to this choice.

The optimized strata of the selected solution are the following:

plotStrata2d(framenew,outstrata,domain=1,vars=c("X1","X2"),
             labels=c("Lead","Zinc"))
Stratum Population Allocation SamplingRate Bounds Lead Bounds Zinc
1 362 8 0.02162891 3.33446915108525-3.97830766572185 4.12033872416343-5.08197020395773
2 912 20 0.02170874 3.98078882695963-4.66295403226958 4.89922567263803-5.41039990204222
3 601 13 0.02134833 4.27306127281303-4.90590922328998 5.41215085205571-5.83650053811594
4 659 15 0.02243168 4.62875272328487-5.23475059497162 5.78500337127683-6.53159656178355
5 569 13 0.02341675 5.02491543543029-6.24785534081567 6.20543959804885-7.39610824963638

that can be visualised in this way:

frameres <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(data=framenew, coords=cbind(framenew$LON,framenew$LAT) )
frameres2 <- SpatialPixelsDataFrame(points=frameres[c("LON","LAT")], data=framenew)
frameres2$LABEL <- as.factor(frameres2$LABEL)
spplot(frameres2,c("LABEL"), col.regions=bpy.colors(nlevels(frameres2$LABEL)))

We can now proceed with the selection of the sample, using the function ‘selectSampleSpatial’ (which is a wrapper of function ‘lpm2_kdtree’ in package ‘SamplingBigData’, see Lisic and Grafström (2018)), in order to ensure a spatially balanced sample:

s <- selectSampleSpatial(framenew,outstrata,coord_names=c("LON","LAT"))
## 
## *** Sample has been drawn successfully ***
##  69  units have been selected from  5  strata

whose units are so distributed in the territory (sampled points in white, over the optimized strata):

samp <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(data=s, coords=cbind(s$LON,s$LAT))
spplot(frameres2, c("LABEL"), col.regions=bpy.colors(nlevels(frameres2$LABEL)),
       sp.layout = list("sp.points", samp, pch=21, col="black", fill="white", cex=1))

In an interactive R session, the selected units can also be displayed on an OpenStreetMap background with the package mapview (the Meuse coordinates are in the Dutch national grid, EPSG:28992):

library(sf)
library(mapview)
s_sf <- st_as_sf(s, coords = c("LON","LAT"), crs = 28992)
s_sf$LABEL <- as.factor(s_sf$LABEL)
mapview(s_sf, zcol="LABEL", map.types = c("OpenStreetMap"))

References

de Gruijter, J. J., A. B. McBratney, B. Minasny, I. Wheeler, B. P. Malone, and U. Stockmann. 2016. “Farm-Scale Soil Carbon Auditing.” Geoderma 265: 120–30.
de Gruijter, J. J., B. Minasny, and A. B. McBratney. 2015. “Optimizing Stratification and Allocation for Design-Based Estimation of Spatial Means Using Predictions with Error.” Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology 3 (1): 19–42.
de Gruijter, J. J., I. Wheeler, and B. P. Malone. 2019. “Using Model Predictions of Soil Carbon in Farm-Scale Auditing - a Software Tool.” Agricultural Systems 169: 24–30.
Lisic, J., and A. Grafström. 2018. SamplingBigData: Sampling Methods for Big Data. https://cran.r-project.org/package=SamplingBigData.
